lines: Picture a road network where every road has its own drive time, and the question is the fastest way from one city to every other city at once.
There's a way to answer that without ever reconsidering a city once its fastest time is known.
But that only holds under one condition: no road can ever make a trip shorter by being driven.
Take a graph with just one negative-weight edge sitting somewhere in it.
Does this algorithm still find the correct shortest distances, or does that one edge break it?
answer: No. A negative edge can make an already-settled vertex wrong.
The algorithm settles the closest unsettled vertex and never looks at it again.

If a cheaper route to that vertex only shows up later, through a negative edge, the algorithm has already moved on. It settled that vertex at a distance a later relaxation could have beaten, and it never finds out.

lines: Here's the mechanism. Pop the closest unsettled vertex from a priority queue.
Settle it — treat its distance as final.
Relax every one of its outgoing edges, checking whether going through this vertex improves the distance to each neighbor.
Repeat until the queue is empty. One settled vertex per round, and each one is final the moment it's popped.
Now watch this go wrong, on the exact graph where it does.
The algorithm settles a vertex at some distance — final, as far as it's concerned.
But a negative edge, reached only later in the search, could have beaten that distance. The vertex is never revisited, so the wrong distance stands.
Lazy deletion and a true decrease-key operation give the identical final distances, on any graph.
Do they also do the identical amount of work inside the priority queue, or does one of them do strictly more?
answer: Lazy deletion does strictly more work. It pushes duplicate entries it has to discard later.
Lazy deletion never removes a stale entry when a vertex's distance improves. It just pushes a smaller one and leaves the old one sitting in the queue.

Every one of those old entries still has to be popped and thrown away later, as stale. Decrease-key updates a vertex's one existing entry in place, so that extra work never gets created to begin with.

lines: This algorithm settles the closest vertex first, and that greedy choice is only safe because no edge can ever make a path shorter by being added to it.
The moment even one edge weight can turn negative, that safety breaks completely, and the closest-first order can no longer be trusted.
Handling that case — and telling when it makes the whole question unanswerable — is next.
